overview: This file brings together U.S. State Department material on Japanese organized labor and employer-employee relations, beginning with the controversy surrounding a government Labor Union Bill in 1930 and ending with an internal 1933 note on labor conditions related to the Singer Sewing Machine Company dispute. Its largest component is a detailed 1934 consular report on the Japan Seamen’s Union, including its membership, finances, unemployment program, relations with shipowners and other unions, political influence, and demands for trade-union legislation, an eight-hour day, improved wages, safer manning, and better working conditions. The accompanying departmental memorandum emphasizes both the union’s unusually Western approach to collective bargaining and the possible consequences of higher Japanese operating costs for American shipping. Although the stated file dates end in 1933, pages 4–17 consist of material from 1934, illustrating the sometimes irregular accumulation or later filing of related records.

subfiles.title: The Thirteenth Annual Meeting of the Japan Seamen’s Union
subfiles.from: Vice Consul Robert Mills McClintock, Kobe
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: A comprehensive consular report examines the membership, functions, finances, politics, and platform of Japan’s largest labor union.
subfiles.summary: McClintock presents the Japan Seamen’s Union as the country’s largest and most highly integrated union, with 98,612 members and an unusually strong position in maritime employment. He attributes maritime unionism partly to seamen’s freedom from older feudal craft traditions and their exposure to labor conditions under foreign flags, then surveys the union’s arbitration work, unemployment relief and insurance, cooperation and disputes with shipowners, political influence, and strong finances. The report reproduces demands for an eight-hour day, wage increases, bonuses, minimum manning levels, improved food and accommodations, retirement allowances, revision of the Seamen’s Code, and a national trade-union law. Its concluding resolution sharply challenges government and employer claims by arguing that Japanese trade competitiveness depended upon low wages and long hours.

subfiles.title: Internal note on Japanese labor conditions and the Singer dispute
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs (initialed EHD)
subfiles.about: A brief departmental note summarizes a Tokyo consular report relevant to labor trouble involving the Singer Sewing Machine Company.
subfiles.summary: Note on a Tokyo report on Japanese labor conditions relevant to the Singer Sewing Machine dispute, calling employment relations feudal.

interest: Shows a 1930s labor-union bill debate, and a seamen's union admitting Japan's export success relied on low wages.
